source.title: From Data Statistics to Feature Geometry: How Correlations Shape Superposition
source.authors: Lucas Prieto; Edward Stevinson; Melih Barsbey; Tolga Birdal; Pedro A. M. Mediano

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own autoencoder and transformer experiments that refine the standard toy-model account: correlated features can use constructive interference and have geometry that differs from near-orthogonal regular arrangements.
record.gate_note: Rows cover reported synthetic and BOWS geometry, reconstruction and feature-group findings, plus value-coding results that fit no listed version. Figure-only geometry is included only where the text describes the result. Cited findings from other work and parameter values used only to choose settings are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own tied-weight ReLU and linear autoencoders, using the original toy-model setup, on correlated synthetic and bag-of-words text data. It argues the standard account of superposition (interference minimised and filtered, near-orthogonal regular geometry) is incomplete when features are correlated. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that with correlated features superposition can exploit constructive interference, arranging features by co-activation. This yields semantic clusters and circles, especially under tight bottlenecks or weight decay, so the interference-only account is incomplete. They also argue such circles can arise from 1-D features, and that value-coding manifolds arise for functional reasons without superposition.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the tied-weight linear/ReLU autoencoder setup associated with the original toy-model work, but trains on realistic correlated bag-of-words text and studies constructive interference, semantic geometry, and value coding rather than only the original sparse, weakly correlated feature setting.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported geometry changes with latent size and weight decay; feature groups also differ in when their structure disappears as latent size increases.

fits_no_version.finding: Value-coding features (city coordinates, Fourier components in modular addition) produce map and circle geometry with uncorrelated inputs. Ablating them collapses accuracy (e.g. MAP 97.94% to 22.43%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Structured geometry can come from task-driven linear value codes rather than correlation-driven superposition.

record.problems: The main empirical setting is a simplified bag-of-words autoencoder rather than a pretrained language model; the authors say BOWS does not capture the full richness of language-model representations. Many geometry results are qualitative plots without numeric measures, and the paper says it lacks a complete mathematical characterization of when constructive interference versus filtering dominates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows beyond the selected reported outcomes. Other qualitative examples and figure panels are not separately recorded where they repeat the same geometry finding without a separate stated outcome.

untested.parts: No sweep of sparsity with iid features, so the sparsity-dependent phase transition is not tested. Results cover correlated features only.
Not tested: no neuron-level polysemanticity, and no privileged basis in the tied AE latent.
Not tested. Value-coding geometry without superposition concerns geometry, not polysemantic neurons.
Not tested: no pretrained LLM and no SAE.
It does not test whether real-model features are 1-D. Ground-truth features here are 1-D by construction.

missing.what: Off-diagonal Frobenius norm of the Gram matrix for months vs Roman numerals across latent size: months become orthogonal earlier, which the authors tie to word frequency giving months more capacity.
Figure-of-eight and spherical synthetic correlation structures: ReLU and linear AEs match at small m and diverge at larger m into sparse interference patterns.
A larger context size C raises the linear-probe FVE and lowers the effective rank, so constructive interference becomes more effective.
Christmas and mbar examples of constructive interference (Christmas one-hot reconstruction about 0.2; beneficial interference in 81% of samples), plus the OpenWebText replication.
Months show structure beyond a 2-D circle (an undulation in PC3).

record.verdict_notes: V2 links were removed: the study measures feature geometry in a tied AE latent with no neurons or polysemanticity. Most results are qualitative UMAP or PCA plots.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not sweep feature sparsity independently of correlation, or test whether the original iid sparse-feature setting has the original sparsity-dependent transition. It tests correlated synthetic features and correlated text features.

It tests capacity-constrained feature geometry in autoencoders, but does not measure polysemantic neurons in a pretrained network or directly establish that important features receive dedicated neuron dimensions.
The paper demonstrates value-coded structure without superposition, but does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise for other reasons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
It does not test SAE recovery or feature spread across neurons in an LLM. Its transformer is trained from scratch on a token-recovery task.
It does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.

It tests scalar ground-truth features represented by directions in its autoencoders, but does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features or establish that real-model features are universally one-dimensional.

rows.subject: ReLU AE on synthetic cyclic-covariance data
rows.operation_detail: Examined learned weight inner-product geometry across latent sizes.
rows.measure: Arrangement of feature directions / weight inner products
rows.baseline: Linear AE learns the top-m principal-component projection.
rows.value: The ReLU AE recovers the circular structure dictated by the top principal components.
rows.note: The text describes a circular, correlation-driven arrangement, rather than near-orthogonal regular geometry.
rows.check: State kept. The features overlap, but the geometry follows the data covariance (a circle), not near-orthogonal regular directions. The baseline is the linear AE's PCA solution.

rows.subject: ReLU AE on synthetic cyclic-covariance data
rows.operation_detail: Examined learned weight inner-product geometry across latent sizes.
rows.measure: Arrangement of feature directions / weight inner products
rows.baseline: At smaller m, the ReLU AE matches the linear AE's circular PCA structure.
rows.value: The ReLU AE abandons the circular PCA structure and represents features as antipodal pairs; ReLU filters negative interference.
rows.note: This is a geometry transition with latent size, but the resulting geometry is not the nearly orthogonal arrangement specified in V1.
rows.check: State should be observed. Antipodal pairs with ReLU filtering of negative interference are one of the original paper's geometries. The text calls this 'one of the cases studied by Elhage et al.'

rows.subject: ReLU AE trained on WikiText-BOWS
rows.operation_detail: Inspected UMAP projections of learned word embeddings.
rows.value: Distinct clusters corresponding to semantic categories are observed under strong compression.
rows.note: Qualitative geometry result; the paper describes clusters but gives no numeric cluster metric.
rows.check: Remove V2: no neurons or polysemanticity are measured, and the AE latent has no privileged basis. Against V1, the semantic clusters are anisotropic, not near-orthogonal.

rows.subject: ReLU AE trained on WikiText-BOWS
rows.operation_detail: Inspected UMAP projections of learned word embeddings.
rows.baseline: Distinct semantic clusters at m = 200, wd = 0.
rows.value: Semantic clustering weakens as latent size increases to 800.
rows.note: The reported change with latent size is qualitative.
rows.check: Remove V2. A qualitative UMAP showing weaker clustering cannot show whether the directions are near-orthogonal or regular.

rows.subject: ReLU AE trained on WikiText-BOWS
rows.operation_detail: Inspected UMAP projections of learned word embeddings.
rows.value: Semantic clustering reappears when weight decay is introduced.
rows.note: The paper interprets this as weight decay favoring constructive interference under compression.
rows.check: Remove V2. 'Observed' described the clustering itself. Against V1, clusters reappearing under weight decay is a departure from near-orthogonal geometry, so partial.

rows.subject: ReLU AE trained on WikiText-BOWS
rows.operation_detail: Compared month-word correlations and PCA of learned encoder features.
rows.measure: Circular structure in the learned month-feature geometry
rows.baseline: PCA of month activations in the data shows a circle.
rows.value: PCA of the learned month encoder features also recovers the circular structure.
rows.note: The paper attributes the learned geometry to cyclic co-activation statistics.
rows.check: Add V6: the circle arises from 1-D binary month features. Against V1 it is partial, because the geometry follows covariance rather than near-orthogonality. For V6, the circle is consistent with superposed 1-D directions.

source_check.correct: V1: partial. V6: observed in this constructed setting; binary month variables are encoded along individual directions and collectively form a circle.
source_check.locator_found: Section 2.2; Figure 4(b–c); Section 4; Appendix J; text lines 205–207, 713–718, 753–757, 3483–3486.
source_check.problem: The shared partial state fits V1 but should be observed for V6 in the tested setting.

rows.subject: ReLU AE trained on WikiText-BOWS
rows.operation_detail: Trained a linear decoder to reconstruct the month inputs.
rows.note: The authors state that none of the months are orthogonal and conclude that the month features are in linear superposition by their definition.
rows.check: For V1 this is partial: the features are superposed (m=1000 < V=10,000) but linearly decodable and non-orthogonal, not filtered near-orthogonal directions. For V6, 1-D features reproduce the structure, which supports V6.

source_check.correct: V1: partial. V6: observed in this constructed setting; the directional month features are linearly recoverable with per-feature R² = 0.98 ± 0.00015.

rows.subject: ReLU AE trained on WikiText-BOWS
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation reconstruction of Beatles-related words with their one-hot reconstruction.
rows.measure: Per-word validation R² and one-hot R²
rows.baseline: One-hot R² is described as near zero.
rows.value: ‘Beatles’ and the band-member surnames have validation R² values above 0.5.
rows.note: The text reports these words as an aggregate example and does not give separate numerical values for each word.
rows.check: Remove V2. Interference is beneficial rather than a cost, which qualifies V1's interference-as-noise picture. Latent size is not stated in the text.

rows.subject: ReLU AE trained on WikiText-BOWS
rows.operation_detail: Compared contextual and one-hot reconstruction for samples containing ‘Beatles’.
rows.measure: Fraction of samples where contextual reconstruction is better than one-hot reconstruction
rows.value: 81% of validation samples containing ‘Beatles’ have better contextual reconstruction.
rows.note: The authors describe correlated context as beneficial interference.
rows.check: Remove V2. Same qualification as R8.

rows.subject: ReLU AE trained on WikiText-BOWS
rows.operation_detail: Applied a linear-superposition test to words, using R = 0.5 as the threshold.
rows.measure: Number of words classified as in linear versus non-linear superposition
rows.value: 4073 words are in non-linear superposition; the 522 most frequent words are in linear superposition.
rows.note: The result shows heterogeneous representation across words; it does not directly measure neuron dedication or feature importance beyond frequency.
rows.check: Remove V2. Most words (4073) are in non-linear superposition, consistent with V1, while the 522 most frequent words use linear superposition.
